## Setup

Run this document from the project root. It loads the packages and the
functions in `src/`.

```{r}
source("src/setup.R")
```

## Simulated dream journal

We simulate 180 nights of one dreamer (`src/simulate_journal.R`). Stress
follows a weekly rhythm; stressful days lead to later bedtimes, shorter and
worse sleep, and a higher chance of a negative dream. Dream texts are built
from templates whose words appear in the word lists in `data/lexicons/`, so
the app can detect themes, emotions, people and objects in them.

```{r}
journal <- simulate_dream_journal(n_nights = 180, seed = 2026)
head(journal[, c("date", "bedtime", "sleep_hours", "stress", "themes", "emotions")])
```

The app keeps its entries and reviewed labels in one snapshot,
`data/reviewed_dream_journal.rds`, which ships with the repository (180
synthetic nights with simulated reviewed labels). If the snapshot is missing,
the app builds a new one from `data/dream_journal.csv`, which we create here
from the simulated nights when it does not exist yet.

```{r}
journal_path <- "data/dream_journal.csv"
if (!file.exists(journal_path)) write_journal(journal, journal_path)
```

## Analysis: do stress and short sleep make negative dreams more likely?

According to the continuity hypothesis, dreams reflect waking-life
experiences and concerns (Schredl & Hofmann, 2003). Stressful days should
therefore be followed by more unpleasant dreams, and stress is indeed linked
to more frequent nightmares (Schredl, 2003). Sleep loss, in turn, makes
emotional processing more negative (Walker & van der Helm, 2009). We test
both predictors in the dreamer's journal:

> **Research question:** Does more stress the day before, and less sleep,
> increase the chance that a dream is negative?

### Data

We use the journal snapshot the app works with
(`data/reviewed_dream_journal.rds`). For every night with feelings reported
*while dreaming*, we look up each feeling in the NRC VAD lexicon (Mohammad,
2025), which rates words from unpleasant (−1) to pleasant (+1). A dream counts
as **negative** when the average valence of its feelings is below 0.

```{r}
snapshot <- readRDS("data/reviewed_dream_journal.rds")
dreams <- dream_analysis_data(snapshot$journal, snapshot$reviews, snapshot$vad)
head(dreams)
```

`r nrow(dreams)` nights have feelings found in the lexicon;
`r round(100 * mean(dreams$negative))`% of these dreams were negative.

### Model

The outcome is binary (negative dream: yes/no), so we fit a **logistic
regression** with stress the day before (1–10) and hours slept as predictors.
Odds ratios above 1 mean the predictor goes with *more* negative dreams.

```{r}
model <- fit_negative_dream_model(dreams)
results <- negative_dream_results(model)
results$p_value <- vapply(results$p_value, format_p, character(1))
knitr::kable(results, digits = 2,
             col.names = c("Predictor", "Odds ratio", "95% CI low", "95% CI high", "p"))
```

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
plot_negative_dream_model(model)
```

### Interpretation

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| results: asis
cat(paste("-", describe_negative_dream_model(model)), sep = "\n")
```

The figure shows the chance of a negative dream predicted by the model for
6 and 8 hours of sleep: it rises steeply with stress, while the two sleep
lines lie close together. Stress and sleep are related in these data
(*r* = `r round(cor(dreams$stress, dreams$sleep_hours), 2)`), so part of any
sleep effect may be absorbed by stress.

**Limitations.** The data are simulated: `simulate_dream_journal()` builds in
effects of both stress (odds ratio ≈ `r round(exp(0.45), 2)` per point) and
sleep (≈ `r round(exp(-0.5), 2)` per hour) on negative dreams. The model
recovers the stress effect, which mainly shows that the method works. It does
not detect the sleep effect: sleep varies little in these nights
(SD = `r round(sd(dreams$sleep_hours), 2)` h vs. `r round(sd(dreams$stress), 2)`
stress points) and overlaps with stress, so `r nrow(dreams)` nights give too
little power to separate the two. All nights come from one person and are not
independent of each other (e.g. stressful weeks), the outcome depends on how
well the lexicon captures the reported feelings, and the result is an
association, not proof of cause. With real diaries from several people, a
multilevel model with nights nested in dreamers would be the next step.

The app's **Your patterns** tab runs this same analysis on the user's own
journal for any period.

## The app

Run the chunk below in RStudio (or `source("src/setup.R"); run_dream_app()` in
an R console). It does not launch while rendering this document. A cloudy
loading screen shows for a few seconds; tap it to skip.

| Tab | What it shows |
|-----|---------------|
| New dream | Write or edit a night step by step: sleep, dream text, feelings while dreaming and after waking, themes, and the people, animals and objects that appeared |
| Dream themes | Themes as clouds (bigger = more frequent) for the last week, month, year, all nights or a custom period, plus stress per theme |
| Emotions | Feelings while dreaming vs. after waking, and an optional 3D valence-arousal-dominance map |
| Your patterns | The analysis above, run on your own journal |
| People & things | Who and what recur in confirmed entries |
| Calendar | Day, week or month view, coloured by sleep quality, stress or hours slept |
| Sleep | Sleep ring, stats, charts, tips and a shareable story picture |
| Search | Search dream text and all labels |
| Settings | Theme definitions, renaming labels, remembered names, export |

The sidebar also has an *App colour theme* menu (lavender, ocean, forest).

```{r}
if (interactive()) run_dream_app()
```

and Social Psychology, 39*(6), 1161–1178.

Schredl, M. (2003). Effects of state and trait factors on nightmare frequency.
*European Archives of Psychiatry and Clinical Neuroscience, 253*(5), 241–247.

dream activities. *Consciousness and Cognition, 12*(2), 298–308.

Walker, M. P., & van der Helm, E. (2009). Overnight therapy? The role of sleep
in emotional brain processing. *Psychological Bulletin, 135*(5), 731–748.
